newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian investors complain about dividend rules.
newsitem.headline: Australian investors complain about dividend rules.

text.p: Controversial changes to dividend taxation rules in the 1997/98 (June 30) national budget will be hotly debated by equity market operators, fund managers, and accountants who plan to meet with government officials over the next few days.
The meetings, to be conducted by the Treasury Department and the Australian Tax Office, will be held in Melbourne on Friday and in Sydney next Monday.

Industry leaders said they hoped the meetings will lead to watering down the planned legislation to ensure that it only affects "dividend stripping" rather than other more legitimate investment decisions.

Executives from the Australian Stock Exchange (ASX) met with Treasury's most senior tax officer, Ken Henry, in Canberra on Wednesday to discuss the new rules which, among other things, penalise investors who hedge a large part of their portfolio by removing franking credits.

The hedging, on markets operated by either the ASX or the Sydney Futures Exchange, accounts for a large proportion of daily turnover and has noticeably declined since the budget was brought down on May 13, dealers said.
ASX managing director Richard Humphry wrote to Treasurer Peter Costello two days after the budget to call for less draconian rule changes.

Humphry's letter said the changes as they now stand will reduce market liquidity, force investors to take riskier investment decisions and have a negative impact on the reputation of Australia's capital markets.

"ASX believes the implications of some of the proposed changes go far wider than what is outlined in the press release dated 13 May 1997 and would have the effect of reducing economic activity in Australian equity business with a subsequent flow-on effect for the wider investment activity," he said.

Accountants, fund managers and other industry officials said they welcomed the key budget reform of ending dividend stripping schemes which have emerged in recent years and which have been big earners for some high profile brokerage firms.

These schemes take advantage of Australia's system of dividend taxation where investors can reduce their tax bill depending on the amount of tax already paid by the company. One unintended consequence has been that foreign investors temporarily sell their shares to a local investor who can reduce tax by claiming the franking credit on dividends.

In its anti-avoidance tax statement, the government said it will deny franking credits to investors who buy and sell shares within 45 days, who are not the long-term owners of the shares, or who have hedged more than 70 percent of the investment.

Anthony Stolarek, a partner at acccountancy firm Arthur Andersen, said the 45 day rule is causing significant difficulty in financial markets and called for modifications as it appears the government has copied from legislative changes in the United States where conditions are different.

"However in the Australian context the treasury announcement could affect 60 percent or more of investors and has the potential to damage the stock market," said Stolarek, who will attend the Melbourne meeting as the representative of the Institute of Chartered Accountants.
The Sydney Futures Exchange, which competes with the ASX in the hedging business, has found a common cause with its rival.

"We obviously believe that any tax leakage through schemes should be nullified. However it appears that the language used to nullify that leakage has had an impact on the overall market," SFE chief executive Les Hosking told Reuters.

"We will do whatever we see appropriate with the ASX to ensure that the impact is reduced down to eliminating any tax leakage through these measures. If we need to make that representation jointly or singularly to Mr Costello or anybody we will," he said.
